newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Report says Pakistan may face coup if woes persist.
newsitem.headline: Report says Pakistan may face coup if woes persist.

text.p: Pakistan, seen facing slower growth and rising inflation, could also face a military coup unless it solves its political and economic crises, a research report said on Thursday.

The report, by SocGen-Crosby Securities, said any delay in elections set for February 3, the possible reinstatement of Benazir Bhutto's ousted government by the Supreme Court, or failure by the next government to implement economic reforms should be regarded as major risks to democracy.
Any of these could "prompt a coup d'etat by the military and end democratic political activity for a prolonged period", said the brokerage house's South Asian Quarterly Economic Review.
The military, it said, had several reasons for backing President Farooq Leghari's November 5 dismissal of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) government for alleged corruption.
It said the crunch came when the International Monetary Fund suspended lending to Pakistan for failing to meet its terms.
"This meant that the armed forces, for the first time in post-independence history, were being threatened with a real cut in their resource availability," the report said.
The rupee lost 17.14 percent of its dollar value in 1996, raising the cost of importing weapons and equipment.

"More significant, the armed forces probably realised that the PPP government's backing of the Taleban movement in Afghanistan was putting Pakistan on a pro-Islamic foreign policy course which would alienate it from the U.S., which has been the traditional ally of Pakistan's armed forces," the report said.
Leghari's creation of a Council for Defence and National Security, giving generals an advisory voice, was prompted by the caretakers' failure to make an economic breakthrough, it said.
SocGen-Crosby said it expected Pakistan Muslim League leader Nawaz Sharif to win the election because he was likely to support the presidency and let the council keep overall control.
But if Sharif managed only a slim majority he would have to seek coalition partners who could block economic reform, again raising the possibility of eventual military intervention.
Pakistan has been under military rule for 24 years of its 50-year history since independence from Britain in 1947.
SocGen-Crosby said Pakistan's weak external position had marred prospects for an industrial revival, which in turn would slow economic growth in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).
It said stabilisation measures introduced on October 22 would cut industrial growth to four percent from 4.8 percent in 1995/96, reducing GDP growth to 5.7 percent from 6.1 percent.
Pakistan is trying to slash its fiscal deficit to four percent of GDP from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
Industrial expansion would be hit by a 40 percent increase in petroleum and utility prices since June 1996, it added.
However, the report said a reasonable cotton crop of nine million 375-lb bales would keep GDP growth above 5.7 percent.
It predicted that inflation would rise to 13 percent in 1996/97 from 10.8 percent last year.
However, it said exports had grown a promising 15.2 percent in July-December, while imports expanded only 3.9 percent.
"The slowdown of imports will continue due to the 12.5 percent devaluation of the rupee since June 1996," it said.
The trade gap would fall to $2.8 billion from $3.666 billion in 1995/96 on the back of a 12 percent growth in exports, it said.
